title: Headwise routing contention characterization for MoE on long-context LLMs
content:
Context and motivation:
- Observed high p99/p999 latency tails in MoE routing workloads with long-context traces (esp. >32k tokens). Existing instrumentations highlight 'router dispatch wait' but it's unclear whether contention is per-expert queueing, per-head fanout, or a mix.
- This doc documents a set of microbenchmarks and production-like traces that isolate headwise routing contention across model families (Llama-2x, Mistral-XL variants, Qwen-180B) under our serving runtime. Goal: actionable mitigations for tail reduction without sacrificing throughput.

What we mean by "headwise routing contention":
- In top-k gating MoE implementations, gating decisions map tokens to experts, and dispatch is performed per attention head group in our kernel. When token-to-expert imbalance aligns across heads, internal queues (per-CU/SM) spike and stall the rest of the pipeline. This becomes visible as long dispatch latencies and inflated stall time in per-op timelines.

Quick summary of experiments (high level):
- Synthetic skewed distributions: Zipf k=1.2, 1.6, 2.0 with constant sequence length 16k and 64k.
- Burst traces: production-like long conversations concatenated (mix of short and long turns) to create time-varying expert hotness.
- Model family sweep: Llama-2-13B with MoE adapters (2-expert), Mistral-XL-MoE (4-expert topology), Qwen-180B-MoE prototype (8-expert).
- Scheduler variants: current contiguous dispatch (baseline), interleaved per-head dispatch (experiment A), per-expert token quota (experiment B), staggered dispatch windows (experiment C).

Instrumentation notes (what we measured):
- Per-request trace with high-resolution timestamps at: gate decision end, pre-dispatch enqueue, kernel-launch, kernel-complete, kv-cache read/write, and post-commit.
- Per-CU occupancy counters (sampled at 100us).
- Microprofile flamegraphs aggregated by request-id and per-stage histograms.
- Profiling captured both CPU and GPU timelines (ns-level on CPU where possible; GPU via CUPTI and our kernel markers).

Key observations (data highlights):
- Under Zipf k>=1.6 the top-3 experts received >65% of routed tokens. This correlated with 3x increase in per-expert queue wait time and a 1.8x p99 latency increase for long-context requests.
- When hot experts were concentrated on a small set of SMs (from our current placement heuristic), GPU occupancy showed large oscillations: high utilization phases interspersed with stall gaps while waiting on long-running expert kernels.
- Llama variants (smaller hidden dims) showed less kernel-duration variance per-expert, so contention manifested as queueing; Qwen-MoE (large dims) had both long kernel times and queueing -> worst tails.
- Interleaved per-head dispatch (A) reduced p99 by ~18% on Mistral-MoE and ~12% on Llama-MoE for Zipf k=1.8, but dropped aggregate throughput 6–10% depending on sequence length due to increased kernel launch overhead.
- Per-expert token quota (B) smoothed tail behaviour (p999 down ~30%) with modest throughput hit; however it increased median latency slightly because tokens assigned later waited for quota windows.
- Staggered dispatch windows (C) (small time-slicing to allow partial completion of long expert kernels) had best tail reduction with negligible throughput impact in microbenchmarks, but required tighter kernel preemption/visibility which is fragile on some HW.

Trace excerpt (informal):
- Example request id=abc123 (Qwen-MoE, 64k context): gate->dispatch: 7.2ms, queue wait: 112ms, kernel run: 15ms, kv-read: 5.6ms, post-commit: 2.1ms. Queue wait dominated. Flame shows long striations corresponding to repeated dispatch stalls.

Root causes (interpretation):
1) Head correlation: If routing gating correlates across heads (same token preferred experts per head), the parallelism we expect is limited; the multiple heads all schedule the same expert kernels -> heavy local queueing.
2) Placement skew: our current expert-to-SM placement puts several hot experts onto nearby SMs to reduce cross-SM copying, but this increases hot-spotting.
3) Kernel runtime variance: Larger expert partitions (Qwen) cause higher variance in kernel runtimes, amplifying queueing effects.
4) Batch formation heuristics: when tokens with similar routing patterns are batched, they amplify hotness; our batching does not currently randomize within short windows.

Short-term mitigations attempted (and results):
- Randomized intra-batch shuffle of tokens before dispatch: p99 down 7–9%, negligible throughput change. Simple and low-risk.
- Interleaved per-head dispatch (A): prototype works but increases kernel churn. Good for tail-sensitive customers as an opt-in flag.
- Per-expert soft quotas (B): effective at extreme skew but can hurt median for some workloads. Useful as fallback for long-tail production spikes.
- Placement rebalancer: moved top-5 hot experts across more SMs -> reduced occupancy peaks but added a 4% bandwidth overhead for cross-SM exchange.

Longer-term recommendations:
- Move to a hybrid dispatch policy: default randomized shuffle + opt-in interleaved dispatch for latency-SLO customers.
- Change placement heuristics to be skew-aware: when an expert is above a hotness threshold (>x tokens/min), spread its replica set across more SMs and bias kernel coalescing to detect repeated hotness.
- Kernel-level improvements: investigate cooperative multi-stream execution or kernel preemption primitives (if HW supports) to let short kernels finish while large kernels yield.
- Batching policy: introduce a small jitter window (e.g., 2–5ms) to decorrelate routing choices inside high-throughput bursts.
- Runtime telemetry: expose 'expert hotness live map' to Console with rolling-window heatmaps so SREs can set auto-fallback policies.

Open questions and unknowns:
- How does the above interact with KV-cache locality? Our read bandwidth can become a secondary bottleneck when many tokens route to same expert repeatedly (we saw increased kv read latencies coincident with queue spikes).
- Is there a tractable way to offload some gating computations to CPU asynchronously to smooth peaks? CPU precomputation introduces staleness risk for dynamic gating.
- What are the implications for multi-tenant Dedicated pools where one tenant's hotness can impact another? (Need cross-tenant isolation experiments).

Action items / next steps:
- [Priya] Run production A/B with randomized intra-batch shuffle on two small Dedicated clusters for 7 days (capture p50/p95/p99/p999). Target start: 2025-12-08.
- [Sofia] Prototype hybrid dispatch flag and expose via config on canary nodes. Instrument kernel churn metrics. Target: 2025-12-12.
- [Evan] Run placement rebalancer at scale on staging for Qwen-180B-MoE snapshot and measure cross-SM bandwidth impact. Target: 2025-12-05.
- [Michael] Draft Console heatmap UI spec for expert hotness and fallback options, include retention and sampling budget. Target: 2025-12-18.

Notes to reviewers:
- Attached traces in linked_artifacts (s3 path) include raw CUPTI timelines and aggregated flamegraphs. Use the flamegraphs to validate per-expert queuing spikes.
- This doc focuses on routing contention; it intentionally skips deeper KV-cache algorithm changes which should be a separate investigation.

Concluding remark:
- Headwise routing contention is a significant contributor to long-tail latency in MoE long-context workloads. Low-effort mitigations (shuffle + quotas) yield meaningful tail improvements and should be rolled out as opt-ins quickly; medium-term work (placement heuristics + hybrid dispatch) appears promising for larger wins with modest engineering effort.
